newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire waits for Mobutu response to revolt in east.
newsitem.headline: Zaire waits for Mobutu response to revolt in east.

text.p: Zaire waited on Wednesday to see how President Mobutu Sese Seko, who cut short his convalescence in Europe after cancer surgery, plans to end a Tutsi-led revolt that has humiliated the army in the east.

Mobutu, who returned home to a rapturous welcome on Tuesday, told supporters he would stand firm against the latest threat to his rule and the unity of the sprawling and anarchic Central African nation although he gave no specifics.

"You know Africa is very sentimental on these occasions," a senior government official said, commenting on Tuesday's mass turnout for Mobutu. "But today is another day and everybody is waiting for some concrete changes".

A close personal friend of the president suggested that Zaire was bringing in military hardware, including helicopters and fighter jets, and enlisting the help of foreign nationals to bolster its demoralised army.

Mobutu himself said on Tuesday that he had returned, against the advice of his doctors, "to handle the serious situation that threatens the territorial integrity and the survival of Zaire and a sovereign and independent state".
He promised "to restore Zaire's tarnished image" but did not say how.
Hundreds of civilians in rebel-held Goma in the east fled the city on Wednesday, saying they feared the arrival of Mobutu could signal the start of a Zairean counter-offensive.
The government and military commanders have been threatening such a riposte for several weeks.

Local newspapers and political commentators predict Mobutu will re-shuffle the senior ranks of the military, bringing into play generals who have earned their stars on the battlefield and not just in Mobutu's Ngbandi clan circles.

Mobutu's close friend, who asked to remain anonymous, said that military hardware, including fifteen helicopters and several fighter jets have been brought into Zaire in the past three weeks, accompanied by 154 foreign military personnel.

He would not specify the origin or make of the military equipment, or the nationality of the personnel, but said some deliveries had made their way to Mobutu's jungle palace at Gbolite in the northern Equateur region, as well as to the eastern city of Kisangani, a likely rear base for a counter- offensive.

An eyewitness at the international Ndjili airport outside Kinshasa, said he saw a cargo plane with insignia from the Central Asian republic of Tashkent, unloading small arms and new military uniforms two weeks ago.

State media have repeatedly rebroadcast Mobutu's homecoming address but commentators and critics say that if he is to capitalise on the renewed support he found among the impoverished inhabitants of Kinshasa he will also have to make political changes.
"We are waiting for a change and we do not want his promises to be symbolic," Augustine Kabuma, a final year student at the university in Kinshasa told Reuters.

Supporters of radical opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi want Mobutu, who has dominated the life of the nation since seizing power in 1965, to appoint Tshisekedi to head a new government of national union.
Supporters of Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo and of Mobutu himself expect a government reshuffle but with Kengo staying on as prime minister.
